newsitem.title: UK: UK court overturns ruling on boy killer's sentences.
newsitem.headline: UK court overturns ruling on boy killer's sentences.

text.p: Britain's highest court on Thursday overturned a ministerial decision to increase the sentences of two young boys found guilty of one of the country's most horrific crimes -- the savage murder of two-year-old Jamie Bulger.

Jon Venables and Robert Thomson, both now 14, were sentenced in 1993 to a minimum of eight years in detention for the assault and brutal killing of the toddler whose body they abandoned beside a railway line.
But former home secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard decided the sentence was inadequate and increased the minimum sentence to 15 years.
A panel of five judges in the House of Lords (the upper house of parliament) ruled that Howard, whose Conservative Party was ousted in a general election last month, had overstepped his powers.
In a majority decision, they said Howard had been wrong in allowing himself to be swayed by a petition of 250,000 signatures demanding a tougher sentence, presented to him by Bulger's parents.

"It is quite understandable that the family of the murdered boy felt very strongly about the sentence to be served by his killers, but it is quite another matter whether the home secretary was entitled to take into account such protests and other media-inspired protests, about the level of the tariff," said one of the judges.
Howard had also been misguided in equating the boys' sentences with those of adults, the judges ruled.

Lord Browne-Wilkinson said the 1992 murder "was a cruel and sadistic crime" which had provoked "public outrage". But he said the home secretary had to be flexible in setting a minimum sentence so that he could take into account how the young killers' rehabilitation was progressing.
Venables and Thomson, both aged 10 at the time of the killing, are being held in separate secure homes and undergoing rehabilitation and psychiatric care.
Both come from poor homes in the northwest English port city of Liverpool, where they committed their crime.
They were arrested after they were identified on security camera film which showed them leading the toddler out of the shopping mall where he had become separated from his parents.
The murder caused shock and outrage across Britain and anguished soul-searching about increasing violence among the nation's children.
Thursday's ruling was the latest of several rebukes Howard has received from the British courts over decisions he made as home secretary.
On Wednesday, Howard stepped out of the contest for the leadership of the demoralised Conservative Party after coming last of five in the first round of voting.
